title: The Standard
titleHtml: The manager standard, written as behavior.
tagline: Unpacking the manager standard: the observable behaviors.
description: A 45-minute virtual session for Vanderbilt managers: meet the Vanderbilt manager standard, learn the witness test that separates behavior from intention, and locate yourself against the standard honestly.
heroLead: The Vanderbilt manager standard names what good managing looks like here, in behaviors a colleague could watch. Today you learn to read it and place yourself on it.
objectives: Name the observable behaviors that define the Vanderbilt manager standard
Tell a demonstrable behavior apart from an intention or a personality trait
Locate yourself against the standard with evidence and pick one behavior to grow
missionTie: Defining the great university of the 21st Century takes managers who lead well on purpose, and a visible standard makes Exceptional Core Operations personal: every team gets a manager who knows what good looks like.

agenda.d: What the Vanderbilt manager standard lists, and why every line is something a colleague could watch.
The witness test: telling visible behaviors apart from intentions and personality traits.
Place yourself against the standard with evidence, and pick one behavior to grow first.

manifesto: Rate yourself on witnessed behavior, then put one gap's first instance on the calendar.

sections.headline: The standard is a list of observable behaviors.
sections.lead: Every line of the Vanderbilt manager standard names something a manager here does, and a colleague could watch it happen. Google's Project Oxygen research reached the same design: what made its best managers good was a short list of teachable behaviors.

source.label: Project Oxygen manager research, Google re:Work

sections.group: In pairs: pick one line of the standard. When did a colleague last see you do it? 90 seconds each way.
sections.solo: Pick one line of the standard and write down when a colleague last saw you do it.

deeper.title: Witnessed in person, or proven by an artifact
deeper.body: There is a second reason the standard reads as behaviors: a behavior is startable. You can hold a 1:1 this week without first becoming a different person, and the doing quietly builds the quality everyone wanted anyway. Notice too that a witness is not always a person in the room. A calendar entry, a written feedback note, or a shared agenda all count, because a colleague could point to them later.
steps: Walk the standard and mark each line P or A: witnessed in person, or provable by an artifact like a calendar entry or a written feedback note.
Pick one line you marked A and go find last month's artifact. If the search comes up empty, you have found your first honest gap.

card.text: Every line of the Vanderbilt manager standard passes one test: a colleague could watch you do it. Holding the 1:1 counts, and so does written feedback. If nobody could witness it, it is not on the list.

interaction.context: Most leadership language describes who a manager should be: caring, say, or strategic. The Vanderbilt standard refuses that, and Google's Project Oxygen research shows why it can. What separated Google's best managers was a short list of behaviors anyone could learn and anyone could watch.
interaction.discuss: Which line of the standard surprised you by being there, and which quality you value most is missing because nobody could witness it?
interaction.q: Quick check: which of these is written the way the standard is written?

opts.why: That is a trait, and a lovely one. Nobody can watch caring; they can watch what caring does, and the standard names those doings.

opts.t: Holds a scheduled 1:1 with each direct report every month
opts.why: A colleague could witness it and a calendar could prove it. A new manager could start it tomorrow, which is exactly how the standard is written.
Belief lives in your head. The standard's version names the visible act: feedback delivered, in words the person can use.

sections.headline: Telling a behavior from an intention.
sections.lead: The witness test separates a behavior from an intention or a trait: could a colleague have seen it happen? A plan nobody saw yet is an intention, and an adjective is usually a trait. Practice the call on three ordinary claims managers make about themselves.
sections.group: Breakout pairs: name one thing you give yourself credit for that fails the witness test. 90 seconds each way.
sections.solo: Name one thing you give yourself credit for that a colleague could never have witnessed.

deeper.title: The gray zone: claims that describe a state
deeper.body: The trickiest claims are states: my door is open, I am available anytime. A state sounds generous and never happens at a time and place, so nobody can witness it. The conversion is always the same: pick the instance. Open door becomes office hours held every Tuesday at two. Available becomes a reply within one working day. When you hear yourself claim a state, ask for its most recent instance, with a date attached.
steps: Write three claims you would make about your own managing this year. Label each one: behavior, intention, trait, or state.
Convert your weakest claim into an instance a colleague could see: a named action at a named time. Put its first occurrence on your calendar.

interaction.intro: Run the witness test on each claim: ask who could have watched it happen, then label it. Managers who make this call cleanly rate themselves accurately in the next section.
labels: Behavior, a colleague could see it
Intention, it lives in your head
interaction.passMsg: You have the witness test. If a colleague could have seen it, it counts; everything else is intention or adjective.
interaction.failMsg: Close. Ask who could have watched it happen. A plan nobody saw yet is an intention, and an adjective is usually a trait.

items.q: A director says: after every project closes, I send each person two lines of written feedback.
items.why: Witnessable and checkable: the feedback either arrived or it did not. Notice how the specifics are what make it a behavior.

items.q: A manager describes their leadership style as approachable, with a real open-door policy.
items.why: Approachable is an adjective and open door describes a state. Reports only experience what happens when they walk through it; that part is the behavior.

items.q: A team lead plans to start monthly growth conversations once the busy season ends.
items.why: A sincere plan is still invisible to the team. Intentions become behaviors the moment they hit a calendar, and this one has not.

sections.headline: Rate each behavior against evidence.
sections.lead: To locate yourself against the standard, ask one question per behavior: when did a colleague last see me do it? Answer with dates. Then give the biggest gap one visible first move. Nothing you type is saved, so answer honestly.

deeper.title: Evidence has a shelf life
deeper.body: Sometimes the witness test passes on a technicality: you did hold the growth conversation, once, in the spring. So add two follow-up questions to every line you rate yourself on: when was the last instance, and how regular is the rhythm? One strong week a year ago is a memory. A modest behavior repeated monthly is what the standard is actually after, because a rhythm is what your team experiences as managing.
steps: Take the behavior you rated yourself highest on and list its last three instances with dates. If the dates take real digging, lower the rating.
Give your chosen gap behavior a rhythm before you schedule it: monthly, or after each milestone. The rhythm is what makes the habit checkable.

interaction.intro: Choose how you rate yourself and what you do with the gap you find. An evidence-based read plus one scheduled behavior is the combination that changes anything by next month.

opts.t: Rate yourself high across the list; you meant well all year.
opts.coach: Intentions inflate every self-rating. You are grading the manager you meant to be, and your team only ever met the other one.

opts.t: Go with your gut, quickly, line by line.
opts.coach: Gut feel beats avoidance, and it still leans on self-image. Evidence is the honest anchor: what happened, when, witnessed by whom.

opts.t: For each behavior, ask: when did a colleague last see me do this?
opts.coach: The witness test, turned on yourself. Dates and instances replace impressions, and the gaps stop hiding.

slots.key: What you do with the gap

opts.t: Note it privately and resolve to be better.
opts.coach: A private resolution is an intention, and you just spent a session learning what those are worth to your team.

opts.t: Tell your own manager you plan to work on leadership generally.
opts.coach: Saying it out loud helps. Generally is the leak: without one named behavior, there is nothing anyone could witness changing.

opts.t: Pick one behavior and put its first visible instance on the calendar.
opts.coach: One behavior with its first calendar entry, witnessable by Friday. Standards turn into habits exactly this way.

heads.strong: An honest read and a visible first move. The gap you found is now a calendar entry.
heads.mid: A real look with a soft landing. You saw the gap; the follow-through stayed vague.
heads.weak: A generous self-review. The standard stayed a document and the gap stayed invisible.

reactions.strong: Two weeks in, the behavior has happened twice where the team could see it. Your next self-locate starts from evidence, and the evidence moved.
reactions.mid: The intention was real, and busy weeks eat unspecific intentions first. Next month's self-locate finds the same gap waiting.
reactions.weak: Nothing changed, which is the outcome high self-ratings quietly protect. The standard can only help a manager who lets it read them.

recap.q: The Vanderbilt manager standard is a list of...
opts: Observable behaviors a colleague could witness
recap.why: Every line passes the witness test: it can be seen, checked, and started tomorrow. That is what makes the standard usable and measurable.

recap.q: Which of these passes the witness test?
opts: I genuinely care about my team
I plan to start skip-level chats
I hold a monthly 1:1 with each report
recap.why: A colleague could watch it happen and a calendar could confirm it. The other three options never leave the speaker's head.

recap.q: An honest self-locate asks, for each behavior...
opts: How would I like to be seen?
When did a colleague last see me do it?
recap.why: Evidence over impression. Dates and witnessed instances tell you where you actually stand, which is the only useful starting point.

recapMsgs.high: You can read the standard and yourself. Now pick the one behavior.
recapMsgs.mid: Solid. Revisit the witness test, then build your card.
recapMsgs.low: Worth a second pass through the three sections before you self-locate.

capstone.headline: Pick one behavior and schedule its first instance.
capstone.lead: Pick the behavior your honest self-locate points to first. Roles only, never names; nothing you type is saved or sent.
capstone.whoLabel: Which behavior gets your December, and what gap did you find?
capstone.whoPlaceholder: e.g. written feedback after milestones; none given since summer
capstone.practiceLabel: Which move do you make first?

practices.name: The witness pass
practices.move: Walk the standard line by line and mark each one: when did a colleague last see me do this? Honest dates only.

practices.name: The first instance
practices.move: Take your biggest-gap behavior and schedule its first visible instance before Friday.

practices.name: The mirror ask
practices.move: Ask one trusted colleague which behavior on the standard they see from you least. Listen, thank them, skip the defense.

whens.out: The move happens this week, on the calendar by Friday.
The move happens before your next 1:1, so the meeting shows the change.
The move happens before December closes, scheduled today so it cannot slide.

capstone.evidenceRow: Afterward, one line: what did the witness test change about how you see yourself?

closing.headline: Do the behavior where your team can see it.
closing.lead: You know the list and where you stand on it. Tuesday covers the Oracle tools that make several of these behaviors visible; Thursday teaches the clarity skill under expectation-setting.
closing.nextTag: Your one next step · This week
closing.nextTitle: Put the behavior on the calendar
closing.nextBody: Schedule the first visible instance of your chosen behavior and hold it. Bring what a colleague could now witness to next Monday's session.
closing.brandline: Schedule the behavior where your team can see it.

facilitator.audience: Vanderbilt people managers and team leads in the Anchor's Edge weekly rhythm. Works for 6 to 40 on a call; breakouts run in pairs. No prerequisites; December opens the Manager Effectiveness theme after November's Transfer Portal month, and this session introduces the standard itself.
facilitator.pulse: Seven days out, send the pulse: 'Which behavior did you pick? Has a colleague been able to witness it yet? What did the honest self-locate change?' Count of managers with one behavior visibly underway is the month's Level 3 signal.

s1.title: Behaviors, on the record
s1.purpose: Establish that every line of the Vanderbilt manager standard is an observable, demonstrable behavior.
s1.say: Vanderbilt wrote down what good managing looks like here, and the writing choice matters more than it seems. Google did the same exercise years ago. Project Oxygen set out to learn what made its best managers good, and the answer came back as a list of teachable behaviors rather than personality types. Our standard works the same way: every line is something a colleague could watch you do. Nothing on it asks you to be a certain kind of person.
facilitate: Read the concept card aloud once, slowly.
Walk the In the room context: being language versus doing language. No quiz in the live room.
Open the discussion prompt; take two or three voices before moving on.
Run the breakout: one line of the standard, and when a colleague last saw you do it.

ask.q: Why do you think the standard was written as behaviors instead of qualities?
expect: Qualities are arguable, behaviors are checkable
It tells new managers exactly what to do
ask.respond: All of it. A quality invites debate; a behavior invites a calendar entry. Goal 2 can only measure what can be witnessed.

s1.debrief: If no colleague could witness it, it is not on the list. That single design choice is what makes the standard usable.
s1.watchFor: Managers reading the list as an accusation. Frame it as a map: it tells you exactly what good looks like, which most of us were never told.
s1.transition: So what counts as a behavior? That line is blurrier than it sounds.
s1.coreNote: Core: skip the breakout; ask for one surprising line of the standard in chat instead.

s2.title: Behavior or intention?
s2.purpose: Train the witness test: separating observable behaviors from intentions and personality traits.
s2.say: Most of us grade ourselves on intentions and grade everyone else on behavior. I meant to give feedback. I am an approachable person. The witness test asks one question of every claim: could a colleague have seen it happen? If the answer is no, it may be a lovely quality, and your team has never met it.
facilitate: Run Behavior or intention? live; everyone plays on their own screen.
After round two, pause and ask who chose trait versus intention; the distinction sparks the best discussion.
Run the breakout on credit that fails the witness test.

ask.q: What is something managers commonly claim that fails the witness test?
ask.respond: Open door is the classic: it describes a state, and reports only experience what happens when they walk through it. The behavior version is scheduled, visible time.

s2.debrief: Behaviors leave tracks on calendars and in records. Intentions and traits stay in your head, and the standard cannot count what stays there.
s2.watchFor: Cynicism about box-checking. Acknowledge it: a behavior done emptily is still weak managing. The standard is the floor that makes the rest possible.
s2.transition: Which brings us to the uncomfortable part: where do you actually stand on it?
s2.coreNote: Core: run the trainer, skip the breakout, take one voice on the debrief question.

s3.title: The honest self-locate
s3.purpose: Teach an evidence-based self-locate against the standard and convert the biggest gap into one visible move.
s3.say: Now you rate yourself against the standard. Nobody sees your answers and nothing is saved, so there is no audience to perform for; the only reason to be generous with yourself is habit. For each behavior on the standard, ask one question: when did a colleague last actually see me do this? Then take the gap that matters most and give it a first visible move.
facilitate: Run the builder; give the room two minutes to make both choices and run it.
Ask one volunteer to share which slot was harder to answer honestly.
Point at the pattern: evidence over gut feel, one named behavior over a vague vow.

ask.q: Why does picking one behavior beat vowing to improve across the board?
expect: You can put one thing on a calendar
ask.respond: Exactly. The standard has many lines; your December needs one. A single visible behavior, repeated, moves your read on the whole list.

s3.debrief: Honest self-locates run on evidence: when a colleague last saw it. The output is one behavior with its first instance on the calendar.
s3.watchFor: Managers who self-locate low on everything and spiral. Redirect to the one gap that matters most; the standard is a growth map and everyone starts somewhere on it.
s3.transition: Quick recap, then you build your own card.
s3.coreNote: Core: everyone runs the builder solo; skip the share-out.

facilitator.capstoneSay: Now make it yours. One behavior from the standard, the honest gap you found, and the first move you will make. Behavior and roles only, never names. Build the card, copy it somewhere you will see it before Friday. Two minutes, quiet, go.
facilitator.closeSay: You leave knowing the standard and where you honestly stand on it. Tomorrow's Take-Off Tuesday is for everyone on your team, you included: the 1:1 templates and feedback tools inside Oracle that make several of these behaviors visible. Thursday's Thrive Thursday works the clarity skill behind expectation-setting. And if you want a companion this month, the LinkedIn Learning course New Manager Foundations by Todd Dewett pairs well with the navigator-led walk-through clinic on the standard. Both optional, both worth your time.

contingencies.if: Screen share or the site fails mid-session
contingencies.then: Paste the learner link in chat and narrate from your own browser; every interaction runs on learner devices without the share.
Run the breakout prompts as 60-second chat storms: everyone types their answer at once, you read the best three aloud.

contingencies.if: A manager gets defensive about self-locating in a group setting
contingencies.then: Remind the room nothing typed is saved or shared, and self-locates stay private unless someone volunteers. Today is a mirror, nothing more; the standard measures behavior going forward.

contingencies.if: Someone asks whether their self-locate feeds their performance review
contingencies.then: Be direct: nothing from this session is captured anywhere. Goal 2 measurement runs through the formal process your HR partner owns; today is private practice at looking honestly.

toughQuestions.q: Will my self-locate or anything from this session feed my performance review?
toughQuestions.a: No. Nothing typed today is saved or sent, and the session has no reporting behind it. Goal 2 measurement runs through the formal process your HR partner owns; today is private practice at looking honestly before anyone else looks.

toughQuestions.q: My team is huge and my calendar is brutal. Are these behaviors realistic for me?
toughQuestions.a: The standard names behaviors, and behaviors scale: a monthly 1:1 exists whether you have three reports or fifteen, even if the shape differs. If a specific line truly cannot fit your context, that is a real conversation to have with your own leader, out loud, rather than a quiet exemption.

toughQuestions.q: How is this different from the competency models we have seen before?
toughQuestions.a: Competencies describe qualities and invite debate about whether you have them. The standard names witnessable behaviors, which ends the debate: either the 1:1 happened or it did not. That is also what makes Goal 2 measurable. The New Manager Foundations course on LinkedIn Learning walks the same ground if you want a deeper pass.

templates.title: Pre-work invite (paste into the calendar invite)
templates.body: Subject: Monday, 45 minutes on the Vanderbilt manager standard. If you have seen the standard, skim it beforehand; if you have not, come as you are and we walk it together. Live and interactive; have the session link open on your own screen.

templates.title: 7-day pulse (send one week after)
templates.body: Subject: Is the behavior on your calendar? Three lines, reply whenever: 1) Which behavior did you pick? 2) Has a colleague been able to witness it yet? 3) What did the honest self-locate change for you?
